title: regional-routing-signal-attenuation-playbook
body:
Goal and scope: This doc captures a practical checklist and decision logic for handling region-level signal attenuation (high error rates / partial network degradation) that impacts routing, DNS TTLs, and egress paths. It focuses on: 1) safely shifting traffic between regions with minimum cache thrash and client disruption; 2) coordination points with networking and platform teams; 3) quick mitigations (soft redirects, weighted routing) and hard cutovers; 4) rollback and verification criteria.

When to use this playbook: Use when we observe region-level SLO degradation for >5 minutes with request error rate or tail latency impacting >10% of requests and originating consistently from a specific region/cluster. Also applies to third-party egress outages (cloud interconnect, CDN) that cause routing anomalies.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
- Confirm alerts: aggregate from Datadog and tracer spikes. Note the region tag (e.g., us-west-2-eu-west-1).
- Verify scope: query request counts and error breakdown by AZ and by edge POP. Command: curl to internal metrics API or check dashboards: /dashboards/slo/region-latency.
- Check KV cache hit rate delta for the region. Large cache-miss spikes mean replays if we shift too aggressively.
- Look at LB health checks and node drain state. If control plane shows node drain, coordinate with release-engineering.

Immediate mitigations (safe order):
1) Apply local circuit breaker: reduce concurrency or reject bulkhead-y endpoints for the affected region to reduce cascading failures. This buys time without shifting traffic globally.
2) Reduce DNS TTL for affected record(s) to 60s if currently >300s. Note: only do this if origin DNS provider supports sub-minute updates and ops has confidence in clients honoring TTLs.
3) Switch to weighted routing with conservative weights (e.g., shift 10-20% at a time) rather than an all-at-once DNS swap. Use traffic controller to adjust weights: update route-policy region-weight us-west-2 => 70%, us-east-1 => 30%.
4) Enable prefix/KV cache pre-seed on target region(s) before large weight increases. This is critical for models with large KV caches; failure to pre-seed causes token storm and increased latency. Steps: run cache-preseed job id cache-preseed-<timestamp> against target pools and confirm hit rate >80%.
5) If DNS fallback is needed for legacy clients, update low-priority A records and add HTTP 301 fallback headers for clients that respect origin responses.

Hard failover (when to execute):
- Execute full failover when error rate in primary region exceeds 50% of requests and degradation persists >15 minutes OR when customer SLA / legal/regulatory constraints require immediate isolation.
- Before hard failover: notify ExecOps, CS, and partner teams via #sre-incident and create incident bridge. Post ETA and rollback plan in the incident channel.
- Hard failover steps: incrementally move weights in 20% steps every 2 minutes while monitoring 95th/99th latencies and downstream queue lengths. If any metric regresses >15% relative to baseline after a step, pause and evaluate.

DNS specifics and pitfalls: 
- Avoid very short TTLs for long-lived clients (SDKs) — this causes constant re-resolution and spikes. Prefer weighted routing + CDN reconfiguration over TTL oscillation where possible.
- If using provider-side traffic steering (Cloud DNS geoproximity), validate how the provider interprets POPs vs. client IP. Misinterpretation can send mobile traffic to far-away regions.
- When updating DNS records: record changes with the provider transaction ID and monitor DNS propagation via global dig checks and DNSViz if necessary.

KV cache considerations:
- Cache warming: pre-seed frequently used prefixes and model KV for the target region. Use the pre-seed tool with a dry-run to estimate prewarming time.
- Cache eviction risk: if target region does not have sufficient RAM/GPUs, we will see high truncation and evictions causing latency spikes; check node memory pressure metrics before scaling traffic.

Coordination matrix (who to notify and when):
- Immediate: #sre-incident, platform-oncall, networking-oncall.
- 10-minute update: release-eng, model-ops, product-ops.
- 30-minute update: growth/CS for customer-visible incidents.
- Legal/compliance: only if customer data plane is affected or region isolation is driven by legal/regulatory reasons.

Validation and post-shift checks:
- Verify user-facing error rate returns to baseline for 10 consecutive minutes.
- Validate KV cache hit ratio in new region >= 75% within 10 minutes.
- Confirm model output quality checks (sample inference requests) against golden prompt set.
- Confirm logs and traces are present and route attributes include region tags.

Rollback criteria:
- If error rate or p95/p99 latency worsens by >15% after a weighting step, revert to previous weighting and re-evaluate.
- If cache hit ratio is <50% after 15 minutes despite pre-seed, rollback.
- If third-party egress shows repeated BGP flaps or packet loss >3% between our regions, restore original routing and escalate to networking provider.

Common gotchas and lessons learned from recent incidents:
- Too-fast DNS TTL changes caused SDK clients to hammer origin causing transient capacity depletion. Lesson: prefer weighted routing where you can adjust at the controller level.
- Not prewarming KV caused token storms and downstream throttles when traffic moved. Always run preseed; make it an automated step in the weight-change pipeline.
- Bumping weights without checking regional quotas led to capacity exhaustion in the target region. Precheck GPU/instance quotas before shifting traffic.

Action items (post-incident):
- Automate pre-seed job trigger in the routing service for any >10% weight move. Owner: Omar Singh. Due: 2026-03-15.
- Add synthetic golden prompt checks to the canary gating flow. Owner: Ellen Park. Due: 2026-03-22.
- Document DNS provider-specific caveats for geoproximity in confluence page CONFLUENCE-REGION-FLOW-23. Owner: Rajiv Menon. Due: 2026-03-10.

Open questions: 
- Do SDKs respect TTLs in all major client versions? We need a telemetry sweep across versions and platforms.
- Can the traffic controller perform automatic staged shifts based on observed SLO delta, or do we require manual ratcheting?

Incident reference example (short timeline):
- 10:04: Alert: us-west-2 latency spike (p99 > 3s).
- 10:08: Triage confirms region-level cache miss spike and increased 504s.
- 10:12: Circuit breakers applied to non-critical endpoints and DNS TTL lowered to 60s for affected A records.
- 10:20: Pre-seed started for us-east-1, weight shift started 10% -> monitor.
- 10:40: Reached 80% traffic in us-east-1; KV hit ratio recovered; incident declared mitigated.

References and artifacts: see linked_artifacts for PR and tickets. Also check internal dashboard: /dashboards/sre/region-failover. Slack thread: #sre-incident-thread-xyz.

Notes to self / quick reminders: keep communications simple and timestamped, record route-policy deltas in the incident ticket, and always capture the provider transaction IDs for DNS and cloud routing changes.

This is a living doc — feedback welcome. If you run through this playbook during an incident, paste the run timestamps and any overrides into the incident ticket for postmortem analysis.
